newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: ZAMBIAN FARMERS SEE NO IMPENDING FERTILISER CRISIS.
newsitem.headline: ZAMBIAN FARMERS SEE NO IMPENDING FERTILISER CRISIS.

text.p: Zambia's National Union of Farmers on Wednesday dismissed reports of an impending fertiliser shortage and possible famine resulting from a suspension of western aid to Zambia.
"There is going to be at least 100,000 tonnes of fertilisers available to farmers this season," union spokesman George Gray told Reuters in an interview.
Gray said Zambia had carried over 10,000 tonnes of fertiliser from last season, plus a further 16,000 tonnes provided by donor countries.
The European Union would provide 25,000 tonnes for sale on the Commodity Exchange, while the private sector was ready to import at least 50,000 tonnes more, he said.

A British newsletter reported last month that Zambia was faced with potential famine because of an imminent fertiliser shortage resulting from the withdrawal of balance of payments' support by western countries displeased by new electoral laws in this southern African country.

It said Zambia needed 50,000 tonnes of fertiliser worth around $20 million, but was unlikely to procure it because the government owed a major exporter $5 million and was unable to provide letters of credit.

Last season, the government provided 80,000 tonnes while the private sector provided 50,000. Gray said the government was gradually withdrawing from fertiliser distribution and handing over the function to the private sector.
However, the government could discourage fertiliser imports if it forced the price down to appease farmers ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections.

"If the government puts cheap fertiliser on the market -- a great temptation in an election year -- it will be to the detriment of the private sector," Gray said. "We have therefore asked the government to say what its fertiliser policy is."
There was no immediate reaction from the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security.
